title: A quasiparticle-protected superconducting qubit
authors: Trond Hjerpekjøn Haug, Johan Kolvik, Joey Frey, Paul Burger, Fabian Resare, Witlef Wieczorek, Simone Gasparinetti, Per Delsing, Raphaël Van Laer
abstract: Superconducting quantum circuits underpin large-scale quantum processors and are increasingly interfaced with optical systems, yet they are vulnerable to quasiparticle poisoning from high-energy radiation and optical fields. Gap engineering of Josephson junctions suppresses quasiparticle-induced relaxation, but quasiparticles near the junction can still shift the qubit frequency and cause phase errors. Here, we extend gap engineering beyond the junction using a flux-tunable transmon with a gold-on-niobium ground plane and island and strongly gap-engineered aluminum junctions designed to keep quasiparticles away from the junction leads. Compared with an all-aluminum transmon with nominally identical junctions, we demonstrate that the niobium device withstands more than an order of magnitude higher near-infrared optical power before excess relaxation appears. The Nb transmon shows no resolvable quasiparticle-induced frequency shift over the same power range. At the same time, we observe that dephasing and state-preparation-and-measurement infidelity increase with optical power even while relaxation remains protected. These results suggest that engineering the quasiparticle energy landscape beyond the junction can substantially increase qubit resilience, not only to radiation-induced error bursts, but also to nearby optical fields.
summary: This research addresses the vulnerability of superconducting qubits to quasiparticle poisoning from optical fields. By engineering the superconducting material's energy landscape beyond the Josephson junction, the authors developed a Niobium-based transmon that resists optical power-induced relaxation significantly better than standard aluminum devices. This demonstrates a crucial pathway for building more robust, scalable quantum processors.
main_problem: Superconducting qubits are highly susceptible to decoherence and errors caused by quasiparticle (QP) poisoning from high-energy radiation and optical fields.
main_result: Engineering the quasiparticle energy landscape beyond the Josephson junction, using a Niobium ground plane, increased the qubit's resilience to optical power by over an order of magnitude compared to all-Aluminum devices.
method: The study involves fabricating and characterizing superconducting transmon qubits under varying levels of near-infrared optical illumination, measuring coherence times and frequency shifts.
model_or_system: The platform is superconducting transmon qubits, comparing an all-Aluminum (Al) device against a novel Niobium (Nb)/Au device. The engineering focuses on controlling the QP energy landscape surrounding the Josephson junctions.
key_observables: Relaxation time ($T_1$), coherence time ($T^*$), QP-induced frequency shift ($\delta\omega_q$), and the onset of excess relaxation as a function of optical power.
important_parameters: Near-infrared optical power ($P_o$), gap engineering parameters ($\delta\Delta$), and the material choice (Al vs. Nb).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that engineering the QP energy landscape can physically separate the qubit from the sources of poisoning, although dephasing remains vulnerable.
figures_summary: Figures compare $T_1$ and $T^*$ degradation versus optical power for Al and Nb transmons, demonstrating the superior resilience of the Nb device. Simulations also model resonator quality factor ($Q$) dependence on QP sheet resistance.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of QP poisoning, details the novel Nb/Au device structure, presents comparative measurements showing enhanced resilience, and concludes that gap engineering beyond the junction is crucial for robust quantum processors.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware limitations in superconducting quantum computing by providing an experimental method to enhance qubit coherence against environmental noise sources like optical fields, which is critical for scaling quantum processors.
